fields.title: Dropping the tasks FS watcher on the sqlite backend is safe — every daemon store write already rebuilds and broadcasts
fields.body: startServer's watchTasks() only runs on the file backend now (a database-backed project has no directory to watch, and the daemon is its only writer). That is only safe if every writer refreshes the cache itself, so I audited all 34 store.update/create/amend/remove call sites in packages/server/src outside api.ts: orchestrator.ts (20), pr.ts (3), plan.ts (4), epic.ts (1), fixLoop.ts (1), verify.ts (1), linear/sync.ts (4). All are covered — each either rebuilds+broadcasts inline, or is a private helper whose caller does (mergeRun/mergeRunIntoEpicBranch via review() at orchestrator.ts:1749; landEpicLocally rebuilds 26 lines after its own write), or is one write in a batch that rebuilds once at the end (plan.ts's epic+tasks creation, LinearSync.syncOnce). So index.ts's long-standing comment that the watcher is a duplicate of the handlers' own rebuild is accurate, and removing it changes no observable behaviour. Worth knowing for the receipts and migration tasks: the invariant "any code path that writes the store must rebuild the cache and broadcast task.changed" is now load-bearing rather than merely tidy, because on sqlite there is no watcher to paper over a miss. I briefly added a redundant second rebuild to api.ts's landEpic handler believing it was uncovered; mutation-testing showed the test stayed green, which is how I found landEpicLocally already does it, and I reverted.

fields.title: Import scope: tasks/findings/ledger move to SQLite; fix-loops, notes and inbox stay file-backed and are counted, not moved
fields.body:
Confirmed by the human on t-880ce2 (Q1=a, Q2=a). Two rules later tasks in this epic inherit.

(1) WHAT MOVES. The one-time import writes only the three record kinds the DB already models AND the daemon already reads from it on the sqlite backend: tasks (epics included, kind='epic'), findings, ledger entries. fix-loops.jsonl, notes.json and .dispatch/inbox/*.md are NOT imported. They have no tables, and FixLoopStore/InboxStore are file-only on both backends, so importing them would create a duplicate that goes stale the moment a fix loop advances or someone types a line into their inbox file — worse than not importing. The import report still COUNTS them and lists them explicitly as "left as files (store not yet DB-backed)", so nothing is silently omitted. Consequence for t-b3ad8f ("shrink in-repo .dispatch to committable config only"): its premise that "the import task already moved their contents" is FALSE for fix-loops/notes/inbox. Do not stop writing those three into the repo until their stores are DB-backed — porting FixLoopStore and InboxStore behind a backend seam (the way t-c6dbd3 did for tasks/findings/ledger) is unowned work that has to land first. Note the inbox is deliberately hand-editable markdown with no timestamps on items, so moving it to SQLite is a format change and a product decision, not plumbing.

(2) ORIGINALS ARE NEVER DELETED. The import leaves every source file untouched on disk. The task text says originals are "preserved into the receipt log", but the receipt log is t-9d89bb and has not shipped; there is nowhere to preserve them into. Deletion belongs to t-b3ad8f, gated on t-9d89bb. So the import is additive only, which is also what makes it safely re-runnable.

(3) AUTO-RUN IS OPT-IN, NOT UNIVERSAL. The import runs automatically at daemon boot only for a project whose resolved backend is already sqlite and which still has a legacy .dispatch/tasks board. A daemon booting on a file-backed project does not migrate it and does not flip its storage marker. Opting in stays deliberate: DISPATCH_STORE_BACKEND=sqlite, or the new `dispatch migrate` command. resolveStoreBackend()'s current blanket refusal of sqlite-over-an-existing-markdown-board is relaxed to exactly that extent and no further.

fields.title: Migration scope: tasks/findings/ledger/evidence import; fix-loops, notes, inbox stay file-backed and are reported, not dropped
fields.body:
Decided with the human for t-880ce2; recording it here so t-9d89bb (receipt log) and t-b3ad8f (retire/delete originals) inherit it rather than re-litigating.

WHAT MOVES (Q1 = a). The one-time import covers exactly the record types that already have a destination table in packages/core/src/sqliteDb.ts: tasks (.dispatch/tasks/*.md), findings (.dispatch/findings.jsonl), ledger entries (.dispatch/ledger.jsonl), and the evidence/mutations rows carried in the run transcripts under ~/.dispatch/runs/<hash>/*.jsonl.

WHAT DOES NOT MOVE, and why it is not an omission. fix-loops.jsonl, notes.json, and inbox/<handle>.md have NO table in the schema today — the sqlite backend serves all three from files regardless of backend (index.ts builds InboxStore/NoteStore from rootDir, never from stores.records). Inventing three tables plus a DISPATCH_DB_VERSION bump inside the import task would mean shipping storage for surfaces nobody has ported yet. So they stay file-backed. The binding part: the migration report MUST count them and print them as "left as files (store not yet DB-backed)", with counts. Silently omitting them is the failure mode this rules out — a report that says "185 tasks moved" and never mentions the 3 notes sitting next to them reads as a complete migration when it is not.

WHEN IT AUTO-RUNS (Q2 = a). Only for a project that has ALREADY resolved to the sqlite backend and still has a legacy markdown board present. resolveStoreBackend's current blanket refusal (index.ts:215 — "already has a markdown task board... using files") is relaxed to permit exactly that case, since the import it defers to now exists. A file-backed project is NEVER converted behind the user's back: opting in is DISPATCH_STORE_BACKEND=sqlite or the explicit `dispatch migrate` command. This keeps the marker file (.dispatch/storage.json) the single source of truth for which backend a project is on, which the CLI and MCP both read independently.

ORIGINALS ARE NOT TOUCHED. The import never deletes or rewrites .dispatch/tasks/*.md or any JSONL. Deleting them is t-b3ad8f's call and exporting them to the git receipt log is t-9d89bb's; both need the import to be non-destructive so they can be built and reverted independently. Idempotency comes from INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on real ids, not from consuming the source.

PARITY IS PROVEN, NOT ASSERTED. The report gives a per-record-type count read back out of the database, and every skipped record is listed by id with its reason (duplicate id, unparseable row, damaged frontmatter). A dry-run against this repo's own .dispatch/ — 185 task files, 229 KB findings.jsonl, 121 KB ledger.jsonl — is attached to t-880ce2 before any real import path is exercised, and `dispatch doctor` must come back green afterwards.

Known trap for whoever touches this next: findings.jsonl and ledger.jsonl are append-only with last-write-wins compaction keyed by `id + "\n" + createdAt`, so two lines sharing an id but differing in createdAt are two DISTINCT surviving records in the file — and they collide on SQLite's PRIMARY KEY. Replaying lines in order and taking the last per (id, createdAt) is required; a naive INSERT-on-first-sight imports stale versions of edited findings.

fields.title: Two agents wrote the same worktree at once: a daemon restart orphaned a run's agent process instead of killing it
fields.body:
Recording as evidence for the resilience work (see e-ac6705 and t-050819 — the dev-build-restarts-dispatchd hazard is the same root cause seen from the other end).

WHAT HAPPENED. Run r-6dd770 (this task) was resumed after a dispatchd restart. The restart did not kill the original agent process; it survived as an orphan and kept working. The resume then started a SECOND agent against the SAME worktree (~/.dispatch/worktrees/cc658f598366/r-6dd770). For roughly 45 minutes both were live and editing the same files. Confirmed with ps: pid 6373 (the orphan, run id r-6dd770) and pid 20683 (the resumed agent, DISPATCH_RUN_ID=r-ab889f), both with --root pointed at that one worktree.

WHY IT WAS NOT OBVIOUS. Every signal an agent normally trusts said the worktree was its own. `git status` was clean at session start. The dispatch prompt's "other agents in this repo right now" section listed only an unrelated run in a different worktree — it reports concurrency across the PROJECT, so two runs sharing ONE worktree is exactly the case it does not surface. The orphan's writes only became visible as a puzzle: packages/core/src/index.ts already exported names from a migrate.ts that did not exist yet. The decisive check was `ps -ax | grep <worktree path>` and comparing file mtimes against the current clock — index.ts had been written 10 seconds before, by nobody in this session.

THE DAMAGE MODEL. Both agents were implementing t-880ce2 and converged on different APIs (importLegacyProject(stores, opts) vs migrateProject({rootDir, ...})). The Write tool's "must Read before overwriting" guard does NOT protect against this: it only fires for files that exist at the moment of the write, so two agents creating the same new file race cleanly and silently. The tree ended up as two coherent halves that did not compose — one agent's index.ts, CLI command, server boot hook and 787 lines of tests, against the other agent's implementation file. Then dispatchd's own wip-commit swept the incoherent mix into a single commit (348a44d5), so `git status` went clean while the tree did not typecheck.

WHAT SAVED IT. The orphan wrote its tests and call sites before its implementation. Tests are an executable spec, so once the orphan was killed the recovery was to rewrite ONE file (migrate.ts) against 787 lines of surviving spec, rather than rewrite six files. All 25 core tests passed on the first run of the reconstructed implementation.

FOR WHOEVER FIXES THIS. Three separable defects: (1) a daemon restart must kill or adopt the agent processes of runs it is dropping — an orphan holding a worktree is worse than a failed run, because a failed run is visible; (2) the resume path must refuse to hand a worktree to a second agent while any process still has it open, or allocate a fresh one; (3) the wip-commit-on-restart should not commit a tree it has not typechecked, or should at least mark the commit as unverified — a clean `git status` over a broken tree is an actively misleading signal to the next agent.

FOR AGENTS UNTIL THEN. `git status` being clean does not mean you are alone in a worktree. If you find code referencing symbols that do not exist, or files whose mtime is newer than your session, run `ps -ax -o pid,etime,command | grep <worktree path>` before writing anything else.

fields.title: Receipt log format IS the legacy file layout, so migrate.ts is the restore path
fields.body:
Asked the human to confirm four shaping decisions for t-9d89bb (layout, default-on, evidence scope, CLI surface); no answer came back inside the window, so I proceeded on my recommendation. Recording it here so the rest of the epic inherits it rather than re-deriving it, and so it can be overturned cheaply if wrong.

THE CENTRAL DECISION. The git receipt log is laid out as a file-backed dispatch project, not as a bespoke export format:

  ~/.dispatch/projects/<rootHash>/receipts/
    .dispatch/tasks/<id>-<slug>.md
    .dispatch/findings.jsonl
    .dispatch/ledger.jsonl
    .dispatch/evidence/<runId>.jsonl
    README.md

That is exactly migrate.ts's LEGACY_SOURCES. The consequence is that the "format round-trips" acceptance criterion needs no bespoke deserializer: restoring is importLegacyProject() pointed at the receipts directory, and a human with no dispatch binary at all can `cp -r receipts/.dispatch /path/to/repo/` and have a working file-backed board.

This was not a lucky coincidence — earlier work in this epic built the return leg deliberately. sqliteTaskStore.toMarkdown() is documented as "the export half of the seam ... how a row reaches the git receipt log", and migrate.ts:155-166 preserves each task's real on-disk filename slug rather than slugify(title) specifically so toMarkdown() round-trips to the filename the repo already committed. Anyone changing either of those is changing the receipt format.

THE ONE REFACTOR THIS FORCED. importLegacyProject() read its sources from stores.tasks.rootDir, which assumes source and target are the same project. Restore needs them to differ (read receipts, write into a rebuilt DB). It now takes an optional options.sourceDir defaulting to stores.tasks.rootDir, so the boot path is unchanged and restore passes the receipts dir. Nothing else about migrate's contract moved.

THE THREE SMALLER CALLS.
1. Enabled by default on sqlite projects (config.yml `receipts: {enabled, dir}`). The epic's premise is that git receipts REPLACE git as the sync layer; an opt-in receipt log makes the "autonomy with receipts" positioning opt-in too. File-backed projects get nothing — BoardSyncer already commits their task files, and index.ts:544 already said the split this way.
2. Evidence and mutations ARE exported, even though both tables have zero writers today (record_evidence still lands in run transcripts under ~/.dispatch/runs/). A table the exporter silently ignores is precisely the failure mode migrate.ts's `retained` list exists to prevent, and the day someone wires those writers the receipts should not quietly lag. This required adding putCommand/putMutation to SqliteEvidenceStore — addCommand/addMutation compute `seq` inside the INSERT, so replaying them on restore would DOUBLE the evidence rather than being idempotent.
3. No CLI. The exporter runs from the daemon (debounced on task.changed, plus one export at boot); the README inside the receipt log tells a human how to restore by hand. A `dispatch receipts` command is a reasonable follow-up but is not needed to satisfy this task.

TRAP FOR WHOEVER TOUCHES t-b3ad8f (shrink in-repo .dispatch to committable config). The receipt log now exists, which was the gate on deleting the originals — but only for tasks, findings, ledger and evidence. fix-loops.jsonl, notes.json and inbox/ are still NOT in the database and therefore still NOT in the receipt log. Deleting those three because "the receipts have it now" would lose them outright.

fields.title: claude-executor.test.ts always fails for an agent running inside Dispatch (DISPATCH_MCP_BIN leaks in)
fields.body:
Any agent that runs `bun test` in packages/server from inside a Dispatch run will see this failure, conclude it broke something, and go looking. It did not.

THE FAILURE. `test/orchestrator/claude-executor.test.ts` → "ClaudeExecutor dispatch MCP server wiring > wires an mcpServers.dispatch stdio entry rooted at the worktree cwd, with DISPATCH_PROJECT_ROOT set to the project root":

    expect(dispatch?.command).toBe('bun')
    Expected: "bun"
    Received: "/Applications/Dispatch.app/Contents/Resources/resources/dispatch-mcp"

WHY. Dispatch launches its agents with DISPATCH_MCP_BIN pointing at the packaged dispatch-mcp binary, and the executor honours that override. The test asserts the un-overridden default. So the test is correct, the code is correct, and the environment the agent inherits is what breaks it. Confirm with `env | grep DISPATCH_MCP_BIN`.

THE WORKAROUND. `env -u DISPATCH_MCP_BIN bun test` — 36 pass, 1 skip, 0 fail. This is the same shape as the existing GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL trap already in the ledger: an inherited env var makes a green suite go red in one specific place, and re-running it identically just reproduces it.

FOR WHOEVER FIXES IT PROPERLY. The test should pin the variable rather than depend on it being unset — delete DISPATCH_MCP_BIN (or set it to a known value) in a beforeEach and restore it after, the way the server suite already forces DISPATCH_HOME in test/setup.ts. Until then, do not "fix" the executor to ignore the override; the override is the feature.

SECOND, UNRELATED NOISE IN THE SAME RUN. test/prs-api.test.ts's "pushes a run-with-PR submit to GitHub as one review" fails at ~200s in an aggregate run and passes in isolation — the known under-load flake, not a real failure. Between them these two are why an aggregate server run currently reports 2099 pass / 2 fail on a clean tree.

ALSO WORTH KNOWING: do not leave a full `bun test` running in the background while you commit. The repo's lint-staged hook stashes and restores the worktree around every commit, so a suite running across it is reading files that move underneath it and its results are meaningless. I threw away one 12-minute run that way.

fields.title: Shrink scope: retire the imported originals + ship .dispatch/.gitignore; do NOT flip init's default backend, do NOT relocate the three file-only stores
fields.body:
I asked the human three shaping questions for t-b3ad8f (how to retire the leftovers, what to do about fix-loops/notes/inbox, whether `dispatch init` should default to sqlite). No answer inside the window, so I proceeded on judgement. Recording the calls and — more importantly — the two things I deliberately did NOT do and why, so the follow-ups are not re-derived from scratch.

WHAT THE TASK'S PREMISE GOT WRONG. The description says "Stop writing tasks/, findings.jsonl, ledger.jsonl, fix-loops.jsonl, notes.json, and inbox/ into the repo; the import task already moved their contents." Two corrections. (1) For tasks/findings/ledger the writing had ALREADY stopped before this task started — t-c6dbd3 made startServer select stores.records.findings/ledger on the sqlite backend, skip watchTasks (a SqliteTaskStore has no tasksDir) and skip the BoardSyncer (its own comment defers to the receipts exporter). So there was no writer left to turn off; what remained was the LEFTOVERS, because importLegacyProject is non-destructive by design. (2) For fix-loops/notes/inbox the import never moved anything — they have no tables, and FixLoopStore/NoteStore/InboxStore are constructed from rootDir on BOTH backends.

CALL 1 — RETIRE IS AN EXPLICIT STEP, NOT A BOOT-TIME SWEEP. `dispatch migrate --retire` deletes .dispatch/tasks/, findings.jsonl and ledger.jsonl, and refuses unless (a) the project's recorded backend is sqlite, (b) the database actually holds tasks, and (c) a receipt log exists with the same task ids in it. Deleting 192 tracked files is a git-visible act a human should be the one to commit, and gating on the receipt log rather than on the import's own report means the check reads the destination rather than trusting the process that wrote it. A boot-time sweep would delete a user's board as a side effect of starting a daemon, with the failure mode being silent and total.

CALL 2 — `dispatch init` KEEPS DEFAULTING TO FILES; --db IS THE OPT-IN. This is the one I changed my mind on mid-task and it is the important entry here. Defaulting new projects to sqlite would make the README quickstart fail on its second line: packages/cli/src/commands/task.ts's resolveTaskRoute discovers a daemon with findRunningDaemon and NEVER ensureDaemon (deliberate — "a read should not leave a background daemon running behind it"), and line 154 throws DAEMON_REQUIRED for a database-backed project with no daemon up. So `dispatch init && dispatch task create "..."` works today only because init leaves you on files. Flipping the default is therefore blocked on a real product decision — either task reads auto-start a daemon, or init does, or the CLI gets a read-only attach path to the database. None of those is a line of plumbing, and none was asked for here. Whoever picks this up: the blocker is not the backend, it is that the database backend has no no-daemon read path.

CALL 3 — fix-loops.jsonl / notes.json / inbox/ STAY WHERE THEY ARE. I nearly relocated all three to ~/.dispatch/projects/<hash>/state/ (beside receipts, which is where they architecturally belong) and stopped because the t-880ce2 decision already scoped this out as "unowned work that has to land first", and because the inbox is deliberately hand-editable — its own doc comment says "the cheapest possible capture is opening the file in your editor and typing a line", which a sha256-keyed path under the home directory destroys. Relocating it is a UX decision, not plumbing. Instead they are covered by the gitignore below, which gets the epic's actual stated goal ("no more findings.jsonl/ledger.jsonl churn in project diffs") without moving a file anybody types into.

THE BUG I FOUND ON THE WAY, AND THE FIX THAT CARRIES CALL 3. Nothing shipped a gitignore rule for .dispatch/dispatch.db to a USER's project. This repo has one, hand-written in its own root .gitignore, which is exactly why it was invisible: every developer on Dispatch is covered and no Dispatch user is. A project that ran `dispatch migrate` would commit its SQLite database, its -wal and its -shm on the next `git add .`. initProjectStores now writes a `.dispatch/.gitignore` covering dispatch.db*, fix-loops.jsonl, notes.json and inbox/, so a database-backed project's COMMITTED .dispatch/ is config.yml + team.yml + storage.json and nothing else. It is written by core rather than by the CLI so the desktop's add-project path (server/src/bin.ts --init -> initProjectStores) gets it too, which a CLI-only implementation would have missed.

TRAP: storage.json. index.ts's comment calls it "a committable file"; this repo's own root .gitignore excludes it. They disagree and have since the marker landed. The shipped .dispatch/.gitignore follows index.ts and leaves it committable, because on a retired project the marker is the only thing telling a fresh clone "this board is in a database, restore it from the receipt log" rather than "this project was never initialized". If you change that, change index.ts's comment in the same commit.

Version pinning binds only once the tool is declared, so a half-migrated `.prototools` silently gives you the machine's version while looking pinned.

fields.title: Verifying a dependency override against a dirty node_modules gives a false pass
fields.body:
Cost me a wrong commit on t-dc926d; recording so the next person does not repeat it.

WHAT I DID. `pnpm audit --audit-level critical` reported one critical — GHSA-23hp-3jrh-7fpw, node-tar DoS, vulnerable <=7.5.18 — reached through apps/site > @railway/cli > tar (@railway/cli pins `tar: ^6.1.11`). I added `overrides: {tar: '7.5.19'}` to pnpm-workspace.yaml and verified it: `pnpm install` exited 0, `node_modules/.pnpm/@railway+cli@5.41.2/.../bin/railway` was present, `pnpm exec railway --version` printed 5.43.1, and the audit went from 24 findings (1 critical, 11 high) to 13 (0 critical, 4 high). Every signal green. I committed it.

WHY THAT WAS WORTHLESS. node_modules was already populated from earlier installs. @railway/cli's package was unpacked and its downloaded `railway` binary was already sitting in bin/, so pnpm had no reason to re-run its postinstall — the exact step the override affects. `railway --version` was reading a binary fetched under the OLD tar. On a genuinely clean install (`rm -rf node_modules && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`) it fails hard:

  SyntaxError: The requested module 'tar' does not provide an export named 'default'
      at @railway/cli/npm-install/postinstall.js:7

tar 7 removed the default export that `import tar from "tar"` needs. There is no version that is both patched and compatible, so no override can fix this one.

THE GENERAL RULE. An `overrides` entry only changes behaviour at RESOLVE and POSTINSTALL time. Any verification that does not delete node_modules first is testing the previous resolution. The tell is pnpm printing "Already up to date" / "Lockfile is up to date, resolution step is skipped" — if you see that, your install proved nothing about the override. Always: `rm -rf node_modules packages/*/node_modules apps/*/node_modules && pnpm install`.

SECOND INSTANCE OF THE SAME SHAPE, same task. After adding `onlyBuiltDependencies` for @railway/cli/esbuild/sharp, `pnpm install` STILL reported ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS — because node_modules/.modules.yaml had cached `ignoredBuilds` from the previous run and the no-op install never re-evaluated it. Same cure. (I checked afterwards: `pnpm approve-builds` leaves no machine-local state in ~/.npmrc, ~/.config/pnpm or the lockfile, so pnpm-workspace.yaml really is the only source and a fresh clone is covered.)

WHAT LANDED INSTEAD. `auditConfig.ignoreGhsas: ['GHSA-23hp-3jrh-7fpw']` with the reasoning inline: @railway/cli is a devDependency of apps/site only, used by hand for `moonx site:deploy`, and apps/site's Docker image copies just server.ts plus a prebuilt dist/ and installs no node_modules — so the vulnerable tar never reaches a running service. `pnpm audit` still prints "1 ignored" so it stays visible in CI. Drop the entry when @railway/cli ships a tar ^7 range.

fields.title: CORRECTION: pnpm 11 renamed onlyBuiltDependencies to allowBuilds and ignores the old key silently
fields.body:
This corrects my earlier ledger entry on t-dc926d, which blamed a stale node_modules cache for ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS. That diagnosis was wrong. Recording the correction because the wrong version is already in the ledger and would send the next person down the same blind alley.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE. In pnpm 11 the key that allows a dependency's install scripts to run is `allowBuilds`, a map of `name: true`. `onlyBuiltDependencies` is the pnpm 10 name and is IGNORED — not warned about, not rejected as an unknown key, just ignored. The install keeps failing with ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS and lists the same packages, and nothing anywhere says the key is the problem. `pnpm config list` even echoes `onlyBuiltDependencies` back at you, which is what convinced me it was being read.

HOW I FOOLED MYSELF, AND HOW TO NOT. I added `onlyBuiltDependencies`, the install still failed, I ran `pnpm approve-builds <pkgs>` once, and afterwards a clean install passed. I concluded the allowlist was correct and the earlier failures were a cache artifact. What had actually happened is that `pnpm approve-builds` APPENDED its own `allowBuilds:` block to the bottom of pnpm-workspace.yaml. The file then had a live key and a dead one and I credited the dead one. The decisive test is trivial and I should have run it: delete each block in turn and clean-install. Without `allowBuilds`, exit 1. Without `onlyBuiltDependencies`, no change at all.

THE GENERALIZABLE LESSON, which is the reason this is a hazard and not just a note: when a config change "starts working" after you ALSO did something else, you have not established which one fixed it. Bisect the two before writing the explanation down. I wrote a long, confident, wrong explanation into this ledger instead.

STILL TRUE FROM THE EARLIER ENTRY: verifying an `overrides` change against a populated node_modules really is a false pass, and that is how the `tar: 7.5.19` override looked green while dying on a clean install (tar 7 dropped the default export @railway/cli's postinstall imports). `rm -rf node_modules && pnpm install` before believing any dependency-resolution change. Both traps are real; only the attribution of the ignored-builds one was wrong.

WATCH FOR: `pnpm approve-builds` writing a second block into pnpm-workspace.yaml. YAML with duplicate top-level keys makes pnpm fail to parse the file at all, so if an install starts erroring on the workspace file after you have run approve-builds, look for the appended block at the end.

Rung 1 does NOT change permissionMode — the SDK classifier's routine auto-approvals stay at every rung; the ladder operates in the DecisionFeed, whose DecisionPolicy/DecisionDisposition seam (decisionFeed.ts:83-87) was pre-built for this epic and is the intended implementation point.

Floor patterns live in ONE place, the DecisionPolicy classifier.

(6) NEVER DEMOTE, BY DESIGN (not floor, just out of ladder): plan confirm (a human always tops the dispatch chain — the anti-Lovable property), epic land onto main (rung 4 lands children onto epic/<id> only), warden action confirmations, ask_user questions.

fields.title: Two dispatchd daemons on one root: the new one relaunches every in-flight run while the old daemon's agents keep working in the same worktrees
fields.body: Seen live on t-9ac0f5, 2026-09-07 ~10:40 EDT. A second dispatchd (pid 8397, port 55734, started 10:39:02) came up on ~/Sites/dispatch while the first (pid 96713, port 55383, started 10:35:11) was still running. The new daemon marked every in-flight run failed and relaunched each as a resume — r-678283 became r-733caa for this task — but the old daemon never died, so its agents (claude pid 6132 for this task) kept working. Result: every resumed worktree had two live agents ~90s apart (r-831d7d, r-b9613a, r-0000b1, r-2df6c1, r-872865, r-654e78, r-dd8511 all showed the pair). This is the r-6dd770 orphan hazard from this ledger, one level up: not one orphaned agent, an orphaned DAEMON with its whole fleet. HOW TO TELL: `ps -ax -o pid,lstart,command | grep dispatchd` shows two daemons on the same --root, and `lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -p <pids>` shows two ports. `run_list` from the NEW daemon lists the old run as failed while its process is alive. WHAT I DID: the tracked run (mine) wrote no source files and waited for the orphan to finish, then verified and committed its tree — the orphan's uncommitted work was ahead and coherent, and killing it would have lost it. FOR THE FIX (e-ac6705 / t-050819): daemon boot must detect a live daemon on the same root (the daemon file plus a liveness probe on its port) and either adopt its runs or refuse to start; marking a run failed while its process is alive is the exact wrong move.

fields.title: Policy config key is `policy.rung` (not the design doc's `policy.autonomy`); floor detectors and approval auto-allow are wired by t-4b72c5, not the engine task
fields.body: Two calls made on t-2c6c71 that the rest of the epic should stay consistent with. (1) THE KEY. docs/design/autonomy-ladder.md names the config key `policy.autonomy: 1|2|3|4`; the implementation ships it as `policy.rung: 1|2|3|4` with an optional `policy.gates: {scope|approval|verify-retry|merge: block|auto}` map of per-gate pins. Reason: t-4b72c5 (floor) and t-9ac0f5 (UI, PolicySection.tsx, already in review) both branched from this task's wip commits and read `policy.rung`, POLICY_RUNGS, GATE_RUNGS and consultPolicy from core; renaming the key now would break two live branches for a cosmetic difference. The semantics are the design's exactly: rungs 1-4 cumulative, scope@2, approval@3, verify-retry@3 (OR'd with fixLoop.auto), merge@4 (only when a fix loop settles `complete`; a bare finished run is never green), effectiveRung = min(project rung, risk cap) with routine=4 / elevated=3 / critical=1, and a per-gate `auto` pin never beats the risk cap. If the design doc is ever amended, amend it to `policy.rung`. (2) WHO WIRES WHAT. The engine (packages/server/src/policyEngine.ts) consults policy for four gates and records a ledger entry + an Activity line per auto-decision. The approval gate is implemented but INERT until an `approvalFloor` detector is passed to PolicyEngine and policyDecisionClassifier — with none wired, tool approvals never auto-allow at any rung (failing closed on a gate that can run `git push --force`). t-4b72c5 owns floor.ts (floorCheckForCommand) and is the one to pass it in index.ts; do not add a second detector in the engine. Also owned by t-4b72c5: pinning `fix-loop-capped` feed items to the floor, the budget-exhausted hold, and refusing auto-enqueue of a diff that deletes outside declared writes. (3) WHAT THE SCOPE GATE CHECKS ITSELF. Beyond the rung and risk cap, a scope request auto-grants only if every path is inside the run's worktree or the project root and not under `.git/` (scopePathsInsideRepo in orchestrator/scopeRequests.ts). Floor-pattern paths are not checked there — that is the floor task's list — but the review's undeclaredWrites scan still re-examines every auto-granted extension. (4) CRITICAL CHILDREN. EpicEngine.fillQueue never auto-dispatches a `risk: critical` child; it writes one `[epic] holding <id> for explicit human dispatch` Activity line per session and leaves the child at `ready`. An epic with a held critical child therefore does not end its dispatch session on its own until a human dispatches that child by hand — that is the intended batch review point for publish/release work, not a bug.

fields.title: Scope requests persist across a daemon restart; SDK tool-approval prompts do not, by design
fields.body: t-b2d83a's title says "scope/approval requests", but only scope requests got a durable home. The split, so nobody re-opens it: a scope request is daemon-owned state (the agent's request_scope call long-polls the daemon), so it can be persisted to ~/.dispatch/runs/<hash>/scope-requests.json, reloaded at boot, kept while its force-failed run is still resumable (resumeBlockReason() === null), and carried onto the successor run by resumeRun — where it is re-broadcast as scope.requested, listed by GET /api/runs/:id/scope-requests, put in the resumed agent's prompt under "Scope requests from before the restart", and re-attached to (200, same id) when the agent re-issues request_scope with the same path set. A tool-approval prompt (approval.requested) is different: it is the SDK's canUseTool callback parked inside the agent PROCESS, which the restart kills. There is nothing in the daemon to persist — the pending tool_use dies with the session, and the resumed session simply retries the tool and re-prompts. Persisting approvals would create a card whose grant nothing can consume. Two consequences for the desktop: (1) pendingApprovals stays event-only; (2) pendingScopeRequests is now also seeded from the list route for every live run whenever the live-run set changes, because an app relaunched after the restart never sees the resume's scope.requested frame. Decided records are persisted too (hydrate keeps them; boot reconcile prunes by run), so a human ruling on a force-failed run before it resumes reaches the successor's prompt as GRANTED/DENIED rather than being asked again.

fields.title: Bun.spawnSync (and node:child_process sync APIs under Bun) can spin at 100% CPU forever on bun <= 1.4.2
fields.body: oven-sh/bun#34069, fixed by oven-sh/bun#44581 (merged 2026-10-05, not in 1.4.2). spawnSync loses its child's exit and busy-loops kevent64 when there's fd churn and GC finalizers run mid-wait. Use spawnGitSync/spawnBlocking (packages/server/src/blockingGit.ts), which run the command on a worker thread, or core's spawnSyncText seam. revision.title: Spec: Dispatch TUI + prune
revision.body:
# Dispatch TUI + prune

Date: 2026-10-12 · Epic: e-4d60de

## Goal

Run Dispatch day to day from a terminal (watch runs, talk to the Overseer, approve plans and approvals, browse and file tasks) without opening the desktop app. Building it is also a pruning exercise: a view that doesn't earn a place in the TUI comes out of the desktop app as well.

Success: a full working session works from `dispatch tui`, and both apps share one smaller data layer.

## Decisions

- **Surface:** a new `apps/tui` package (Bun, FSL-1.1-ALv2) built on `@opentui/react`.
- **Data layer:** reuses `@dispatch/client`, the same data layer as the desktop app.
- **Launch:** `dispatch tui` in `packages/cli`. The CLI stays Node-runnable and MIT.
- **Planning:** happens inside the Overseer. The Overseer already proposes one `create_plan` card, and approving a plan that creates a milestone starts its agents (#126). There's no Plans page in either app.
- **Pruning applies to both apps.**

### View inventory

| View | Desktop | TUI |
|---|---|---|
| Overseer (plans and drafts as inline cards), Tasks, Runs (merged Live / AllAgents / SessionsHub), Diff | keep | v1 |
| Docs, Threads | keep | yes |
| PR review, Projects | keep | yes |
| Team | keep | later |
| Files, Terminals | keep | no |
| Setup, FirstRun, SignIn, Settings | keep | no (`dispatch doctor` / CLI config) |
| Draft (AI draft review + first-task guide) | keep for now; moves into the Overseer later | no |
| Plans, BrainDump, Branches, MilestoneBranches, Impact, Design, Gallery | **cut** | no |

Brain dump's notes (quick captures and agents' `dispatch_note` items) move into the Overseer's Coming in column. File links that opened Impact open the Files page instead.

## Architecture

- `dispatch tui` (packages/cli, Node) calls `ensureDaemon(root)` and spawns `bun` on the TUI entry with `--root` and `--port`. Tokens travel in the environment, never argv.
- `apps/tui` (Bun, FSL, `@opentui/react`) renders the shell (header, views, status line, one keymap) and the views.
- `@dispatch/client` is shared with the desktop app: the API client, the Overseer session, gates, models and storage.
- The CLI owns daemon discovery and startup. The TUI never starts a daemon.
- A crash or quit loses nothing, because the TUI only renders daemon state.

## Layout and keymap

- **Overseer:** Coming in | conversation | Going out. Under 120 columns the side columns collapse into header counts and open as overlays with `[` and `]`.
- **Keys:**
  - `1`–`6` switch views (overseer, tasks, runs, docs, threads, PRs); `ctrl+p` opens the project picker; `?` shows help; `q` / `ctrl+c` quit.
  - `tab` moves between columns; `j` / `k` move within a list; `enter` opens.
  - `i` or `/` focuses the composer and `esc` leaves it. While composing, every letter is typed.
  - `y` / `n` act only on a focused proposal card.
  - `d` shows the diff in Runs and PRs.

## Data flow

Pure logic and the Overseer session move into `@dispatch/client` behind a `KeyValueStore`. The desktop binds that to `localStorage` and the TUI to `~/.config/dispatch/tui.json`. Don't move `useDispatchProject` wholesale; the desktop moves onto shared hooks over time. Each app holds one WS connection that invalidates exactly what an event touched, and every reconnect refetches.

## Testing

- **Shared core:** the moved tests move with it.
- **TUI:** frame and keypress tests through OpenTUI's `testRender` at 120×40 and 80×24.
- **Prune:** typecheck, knip, view tests and e2e.
- **Live checks:** only against a sandbox daemon on a separate root and port.

## Sequencing

| # | Task | Sub-project |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | t-c261fe | Desktop prune (#132) |
| 1 | t-43f279 | Shared core extraction (#135) |
| 2 | t-65b62d | TUI v1 and `dispatch tui` (#137) |
| 3 | t-993818 | Docs, Threads, PRs, project picker (#138) |
| — | t-c816ed | Overseer plans unprompted for multi-task messages (#134) |

## As built (2026-10-12, all merged)

- **Runs from source:** the TUI runs from `apps/tui/src/main.tsx` under Bun. `dispatch tui` resolves the entry from `DISPATCH_TUI_ENTRY` or from the checkout the running CLI belongs to, and never from an ancestor directory.
- **App token:** the Overseer, decisions and threads are human-tier. `dispatch tui` reads `DISPATCH_APP_TOKEN` or prompts for it with input hidden (`--ask-token`). Without it the TUI is read-only. Switching to another project via `ctrl+p` is read-only too.
- **Server routes:** routes only the cut views used were kept. Their removal is follow-up t-671e56, because `/api/git/*` is the sample route in several security tests.
- **Untrusted text:** all external text (agent output, PR comments, docs, threads, diffs) is stripped of terminal control sequences before drawing.
- **Pins:** OpenTUI is pinned at 0.5.14, the newest version past the 7-day release-age gate.

## Out of scope

- Settings, setup, Files and Terminals in the TUI.
- Team view in the TUI.
- A compiled binary.
- A team web version.

# Remote connections — plan (t-7e47ccf7)

Scope chosen by wsoule679 (2026-10-21): option A, all four pieces.

## Relationship to other tasks
- **t-5590b68a (mobile app)** and the *mobile-approval* half of **t-70f6f8** build on this: a phone reaches a daemon with the same pairing code → device token.
- The *remote executor* half of t-70f6f8 (agents + worktrees on SSH hosts, driven by the local daemon) is independent of this layer.

## 1. Pairing (server, FSL — not team/)
- `packages/server/src/devices.ts`: `PairedDevices` — the operator's own devices. Each: id, name, tier, sha256 hash, pairedAt, lastUsedAt. File `0600`, same atomic-write pattern as team tokens. Identity = **operator handle** (a device is the owner acting from elsewhere), so it takes **no team seat** and is not a teammate token.
- `PairingCodes`: in-memory, one-time, 10-min TTL, `XXXX-XXXX` Crockford base32. After 10 wrong redemptions every open code is burned (brute-force guard).
- `TokenRegistry` lookup order: built-in → devices → teammates.
- Routes:
  - `POST /api/pair/offer {tier?, name?}` — **owner credential (app token) only**: a decide-tier teammate must not mint a device that speaks for the owner. Returns `{code, expiresAt, tier, origins}`.

# Outside-user requests: intake links and status pages

Task t-020803d2. Decided by Wyat on 2026-10-20: build the spec and phase 1 in this run (1b). Serve the pages from dispatchd now, with app.dispatch.foo hosting them later on the same contract (2c). Outside people get no account, and a capability link is their identity (3a).

## Problem

Someone outside the dev team (a customer, a PM at another company, a teammate without Dispatch) wants to ask the team for a change and then follow it. Today only an *agent* can do this. An A2A client sends a `handoff`. Dispatch drafts a task, the owner approves or declines it in Needs you, and the client follows a mapped A2A state over tasks/get, SSE or push. A *person* has no front door: no form, no page they can read, no updates.

## Approach: a human layer over the A2A handoff path

Phase 1 adds no new intake pipeline. Every human request **is** an A2A handoff from one A2A client that the owner already registered, so the following are reused unchanged:

- the draft shape: an untrusted fence, the `a2a` label, `risk: critical`, and a priority that cannot jump the queue (`packages/a2a/src/draft.ts`)
- the owner's approve/decline `task-proposal` gate in Needs you (`packages/server/src/a2a/handoff.ts`)
- the dispatch guard that holds an unapproved draft (`guards.ts`)
- `policy.handoffsPerDay`, the per-client durable limits, and `port.admit`
- the status projection `decideState` (`packages/a2a/src/projection.ts`)

The new code is limited to three pieces:

1. An **intake link**: an unguessable URL bound to one approved A2A client.
2. A **request receipt**: an unguessable status URL handed to the person after they submit.
3. Human-readable **pages**, plus a webhook event when a request's stage changes.

Everything enters through `BridgePort` (`open`, `facts`, `continue`). That keeps a later hosted implementation (app.dispatch.foo through the relay) on the same seam: the hosted site would call the same port over the relay's call frames.

## Identity of outside users

- **No account in phase 1.** Each submission mints a 32-byte random **status token**. Only its sha256 is stored, in `intake_requests.status_hash`. Holding the URL is the identity: whoever has it can read the status and reply to a question the team asked. Nothing else is reachable with it.
- The form asks for a **name** (required) and a **contact** (optional, free text, typically an email). Neither is verified. Both go into the draft's untrusted fence as `From: <name> (<contact>)`, so the team sees who asked and treats it as a claim, not an identity.
- The **intake link** is a separate 32-byte token, also stored hashed (`intake_links.token_hash`). It can only *submit*. Revoking it stops new submissions, and existing status URLs keep working.
- Every request from one link is attributed in Dispatch to that link's A2A client (`agent:<owner>/a2a.<name>`). Revoking the client stops new submissions from all its links. Its status pages still read, because facts are read through the port without re-authenticating.
- **The spam control is the owner's gate**, as for any handoff: nothing runs until a human approves. The defences are an IP limiter on unknown tokens (the listener's `IpLimiter`, with a lockout after repeated misses), a per-IP page rate, and the client's `handoffsPerDay`.
- **Phase 2 (hosted):** app.dispatch.foo adds an email magic link before submit. The verified email becomes the identity, one person can list all their requests, and email notifications work. The status token stays as the share link.

## What the requester sees

The status page shows **only** the following:

- the request title (the Dispatch task title)
- a five-step tracker (Received → Accepted → In progress → In review → Done) with the current step marked
- one status sentence
- when it last changed
- the PR link once one is open
- the team's latest message in the request's thread, if any
- a reply box while the team has asked a question

The steps map from the existing A2A decision. The page never re-derives status from Dispatch tasks itself.

| A2A decision | Page headline |
| --- | --- |
| AUTH_REQUIRED, draft not yet approved | Received — waiting for the team to accept it |
| AUTH_REQUIRED, approved (another gate) | In progress — waiting on the team |
| SUBMITTED | Accepted — queued |
| WORKING (no stage) | In progress |
| WORKING, stage `review` | In review |
| WORKING, stage `landing` | Landing |
| INPUT_REQUIRED | The team has a question for you (plus a reply box) |
| COMPLETED | Done |
| REJECTED | Declined (plus the owner's reason when given) |
| CANCELED | Withdrawn |
| FAILED | Closed |

The page **never** shows: the transcript, the diff, findings, evidence, agent or teammate names, internal comments, the repo path, or the task id. The team can still share a run deliberately with `dispatch share` (e-dff6d3) and paste that link in a reply.

## Notifications

- **The page** refreshes itself every 30 s while the request is open, and stops once it is terminal.
- **Webhook `request.changed`.** On each change of the requester-visible stage, dispatchd POSTs to the existing `notifications.webhook`:

  ```json
  {
    "event": "request.changed",
    "sentAt": "...",
    "project": { "rootDir": "..." },
    "request": {
      "id": "...",
      "link": "...",
      "task": "...",
      "title": "...",
      "step": "...",
      "headline": "...",
      "name": "...",
      "contact": "...",
      "statusUrl": "..."
    }
  }
  ```

  - The payload carries the requester's contact and status URL on purpose, so an owner's automation (Zapier, a Slack workflow, a mail script) can email the requester.
  - The webhook is the owner's own channel. Anyone who can read it could already see the task.
  - Delivery is at most once per stage. The last notified step is persisted in `intake_requests.notified_step`, so a restart does not re-send.
  - The initial `received` step counts as a change, so the owner hears about new requests too. The Needs you gate also covers that.
- **Email:** phase 2, from the hosted site. dispatchd has no mail sender and should not gain one.

## Surfaces (phase 1)

**Pages on the A2A listener** (`packages/server/src/a2a/listener.ts`). These run on the same port and TLS as A2A, and the relay is not involved:

- `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, so the capability URL does not leak through the PR link
- `Cache-Control: no-store`
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`

- Every field is HTML-escaped.
- The access log redacts tokens (`/r/…`, `/s/…`).
- An unknown token answers the same 404 page as a revoked link, and counts toward the IP lockout.

- `GET /api/a2a/intake`
- `POST /api/a2a/intake` with `{ client, label }` returns `{ id, url, token }` once; the token is never shown again

- `dispatch a2a intake list`
- `dispatch a2a intake revoke <id>`

```

dispatch a2a intake add web-form --label "Feature requests"
```

- `intake_links(id, client, label, token_hash UNIQUE, created_by, created_at, revoked_at)`
- `intake_requests(id, link_id, task_id, status_hash UNIQUE, name, contact, notified_step, created_at)`

`task_id` is the A2A task id (the handoff's root message).

## Out of scope for phase 1

- Hosting through the relay (`/t/<thumbprint>`): the relay forwards port calls, not pages. This is phase 2 on app.dispatch.foo.
- Requester accounts, email verification, and a "my requests" list.
- Attachments, and custom form fields per link.
- Fixing the Needs you grouping bugs t-c854e7 and t-c873e4. Intake requests arrive as handoff proposals, so those fixes apply to them as is.

## Acceptance (phase 1)

- An owner can mint an intake link for an approved A2A client, list it, and revoke it.
- A person submitting the form gets a status URL. The team sees a draft with the `a2a` label and the person's name and contact in its fence, and a task-proposal gate in Needs you.

- When the team asks the requester a question, the page shows it with a reply box, and a reply answers it.
- A revoked link and an unknown token both 404. A revoked link's existing status pages still read.
- Tokens never appear in the access log. Page headers include the CSP and `no-referrer`.
- `request.changed` posts once per step change and survives a restart without re-sending.

# Mobile: monitor runs, answer questions and approve from a phone

Task t-5590b68a. Related: t-70f6f8, which covers running agents on remote machines with mobile approvals. This spec is the phone half of that task. Pairing comes from t-7e47ccf7.

Status: **direction taken, building.** The daemon was down when this was written, so nobody could confirm the choices below. They are the agent's best judgement and are listed under "Decisions" so they can be overturned cheaply.

## Minimum

From a phone, a person can:

1. See their runs: which are running, waiting on them, failed or ready to review, plus the task title.
2. Answer an agent's blocking question, either by picking one of its choices or by typing free text.
3. Approve or deny a gate: a parked tool call, a scope request or an agent registration.
4. Get a push notification when something new needs them, even with the app closed.

Out of scope for v1: dispatching or editing tasks, diffs, review and land, terminals, the board, and teammates' runs.

## What already exists

- **Everything that needs a human is a blocking question message.** This covers agent `msg_send` questions, `scope` gates, `tool-approval` gates and `agent-registration` gates.
  - `GET /api/decisions/open` lists them.
  - `POST /api/messages/:id/reply` answers them.
  - The phone needs no new approval semantics, only a new surface.
- **A `decide` credential is a deciding human.** `resolvePrincipal` maps a registry identity at `decide` tier or above to `human:<handle>` with `canDecide: true`.
- **dispatchd already serves the desktop web bundle.** It falls back to the SPA entry for unknown paths.

## Native or PWA: a PWA

The phone app is a PWA served by the user's own dispatchd and installed with "Add to Home Screen".

- **Why it covers the minimum.** Web Push works for installed PWAs on iOS 16.4 and later and in Android Chrome, which covers all four requirements.
- **What it avoids.** No App Store or Play review, no APNs or FCM account, no signing. It ships with the daemon, so it never drifts out of version with it.
- **Cost.** iOS gets no actionable notifications: inline reply and action buttons need native code, and there is no background refresh. A notification tap opens the decision, so an answer is two taps away. A native shell (Capacitor or Tauri mobile) can wrap the same PWA later.

## Where the UI lives

The UI is a second Vite entry in the desktop app, `apps/desktop/m/index.html` with its code in `apps/desktop/src/mobile/`, so the phone does not download the desktop app.

- It has its own `manifest.webmanifest`.
- It has a service worker scoped to `/m/`.
- It reuses the `@/ui` primitives and the design tokens.

It shows:

- **Needs you:** open decisions, newest first. Each card shows the question, its choices as buttons, a free-text reply field, and Approve/Deny for gates.
- **Runs:** live runs first, then recent finished runs, each with its state and task title.
- **This device:** whether notifications are on, plus "forget this phone".

v1 refreshes by polling every 5 seconds while the page is visible. It does not use the event WebSocket, because mobile browsers drop sockets as soon as a page is backgrounded, and push covers the time the page is closed.

## How the phone reaches the daemon

The phone needs **HTTPS** to reach the daemon, because service workers and push only work in a secure context.

### A dedicated mobile listener

The mobile listener is off by default. It turns on with `PUT /api/mobile/settings { port, publicUrl }` (operator tier), which is kept in `~/.dispatch/projects/<key>/mobile/settings.json` and applied live, or with dispatchd's one-boot `--mobile-port` / `--mobile-url` flags.

- It binds `127.0.0.1` on its own port.
- It serves only `/m/*`, `/assets/*`, pairing (`POST /api/pair`) and an allowlist of API routes.
- It accepts only paired-device tokens, as a bearer header. It never reads cookies.
- It never injects a token and never sends CORS headers.
- It forwards to `handleApi` with Origin and Cookie stripped.

It must be separate from the main listener because every easy way to reach a laptop from a phone delivers requests **from loopback**: `tailscale serve`, `cloudflared`, a local Caddy and an SSH `-L` forward all do. On the main listener a loopback request is trusted and gets the agent token inlined into `index.html`. A tunnel pointed at the main port would hand that token to anyone who can reach the tunnel. With a separate listener, the setup people will reach for is also the safe one.

### Supported paths, in the order the docs give them

1. **Tailscale** (`tailscale serve --bg --https=443 http://127.0.0.1:<port>`). The phone joins the tailnet and HTTPS is automatic. This is the recommended path.
2. **Any tunnel or reverse proxy** the user already runs, such as Cloudflare Tunnel or Caddy.

Later (v2), the phone reaches the daemon through the hosted team site (`app.dispatch.foo`) over the daemon's existing outbound relay socket, so no tunnel is needed. That depends on MCP-mesh piece 4 and lives in the private relay repo.

## Pairing: the daemon's paired devices (t-7e47ccf7)

Pairing is not built here. t-7e47ccf7, which connects the app to a remote dispatchd, adds paired devices to the daemon, and the phone uses the same mechanism a remote desktop does:

- **Offer.** `dispatch pair --tier decide` (or `POST /api/pair/offer`) mints a one-time `XXXX-XXXX` code that lasts 10 minutes. Only the operator in person can mint one, never above their own tier.
- **Redeem.** `POST /api/pair { code, name }` is an open route. It answers `{ token, device, handle, tier }`, and 10 wrong codes burn every open code.
- **Identity.** A device speaks for the operator's handle, takes no team seat, and resolves to `TokenIdentity.device = "d-<8hex>"`. It is revoked with `DELETE /api/devices/:id`.

This spec adds three things on top:

1. **Pairing through the mobile listener.** It forwards `POST /api/pair` unauthenticated, so a phone pairs over the tunnel it will use from then on.
2. **Stricter limits than the tier.** On the mobile listener, a device of any tier reaches only the allowlist below. A phone should be paired at `decide`. It never needs `operator`, and the allowlist holds even if it was paired with that.
3. **A pairing link** (follow-up, once t-7e47ccf7 lands). The offer response gains a `mobileUrl` of `<publicUrl>/m/#pair=<code>`. The code rides in the fragment, which browsers never send, so it never reaches a proxy log. Desktop and the CLI show it as a QR code. Until then the phone page accepts the code typed in.

## Push

Push is standard Web Push: RFC 8030, VAPID (RFC 8292), and aes128gcm payload encryption (RFC 8291). It is built on `node:crypto` with no new dependency, and tested against RFC 8291's worked example byte for byte.

- **Keys and subscriptions.**
  - The daemon generates a VAPID keypair once and stores it in `~/.dispatch/projects/<key>/mobile/vapid.json` with mode 0600.
  - `GET /api/mobile/push/key` serves the public key.
  - The service worker subscribes and posts the subscription to `POST /api/mobile/push/subscriptions`, where it is stored against the caller's `TokenIdentity.device`.
- **Triggers.**
  - A new blocking question addressed to the operator.
  - A run ending `failed` or `interrupted-dirty`.
  - A run reaching `finished` that was seen running and is not yet reviewed.
  - The first snapshot after boot only seeds the baseline.
- **Coalescing.** Within 10 seconds of a push, further events are held and sent as one summary. A single topic means an offline phone gets only the latest.
- **Payload privacy.** The payload is end-to-end encrypted, but Apple and Google still see its size and timing. It carries only `{ kind, id, title, body }`. The title is the gate type and the run's task title or the asking agent, never the question body or the tool input.
- **Delivery.**
  - A `404` or `410` from the push service deletes the subscription.
  - Delivery is best effort with no retry queue. The Needs-you list is the source of truth.
- **No reachability needed.** Push is outbound from the daemon, so it arrives even while the phone cannot reach the daemon. Answering still needs the tunnel.

## API surface (new)

| Route | Who | Listener |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET/PUT /api/mobile/settings` | operator | main |
| `GET /api/mobile/me`, `GET /api/mobile/push/key` | a paired device | both |
| `POST/DELETE /api/mobile/push/subscriptions` | a paired device | both |
| `POST /api/pair` (t-7e47ccf7) | open, code-gated | both |
| `GET /api/decisions/open`, `POST /api/messages/:id/reply`, `GET /api/runs` | a paired device at decide | mobile allowlist |

## Build slices

1. **Mobile listener:** its allowlist and settings.
2. **Push:** VAPID keys, RFC 8291 encryption, the subscription store, triggers and coalescing.
3. **PWA:** the `/m` entry, manifest, service worker and the screens above.
4. **After t-7e47ccf7 lands:**
   - add `mobileUrl` to the pair offer;
   - drop a revoked device's subscriptions;
   - add a QR code in desktop Settings → Mobile and in `dispatch pair`.
5. **Follow-up:** reaching the daemon through `app.dispatch.foo` (v2).

## Decisions (taken by the agent; overturn here)

1. PWA rather than native for v1.
2. v1 is reached through a user-provided HTTPS tunnel (Tailscale recommended) to a dedicated mobile listener. The hosted site route comes in v2.
3. On the mobile listener a phone reaches only the allowlist: it can watch and answer, but not dispatch or land. Pair it at `decide`.
4. Polling rather than the event socket in the PWA.
5. Pairing and device tokens are t-7e47ccf7's paired devices. Push, the listener and the web app key on `TokenIdentity.device`.

  - The payload carries the requester's contact on purpose, so an owner's automation (Zapier, a Slack workflow, a mail script) can email the requester. `statusUrl` is only on the first (`received`) event: dispatchd keeps only the token's hash, so the URL exists only at submission. Later events correlate by `request.id`.
  - The webhook is the owner's own channel. Anyone who can read it could already see the task.
  - Delivery is at most once per stage. The last notified step is persisted in `intake_requests.notified_step`, so a restart does not re-send.
  - The initial `received` step counts as a change, so the owner hears about new requests too. The Needs you gate also covers that.
- **Email:** phase 2, from the hosted site. dispatchd has no mail sender and should not gain one.

## Surfaces (phase 1)

**Pages on the A2A listener** (`packages/server/src/a2a/listener.ts`). These run on the same port and TLS as A2A, and the relay is not involved:

- `GET /r/<linkToken>` serves the form. `POST /r/<linkToken>` takes form-encoded `title`, `details`, `name` and `contact`, calls `port.open` with `kind: handoff`, mints a status token, and answers `303` to `/s/<statusToken>`.
- `GET /s/<statusToken>` serves the status page. `POST /s/<statusToken>` takes `body` (and an optional `choice`), calls `port.continue`, and answers `303` back to the page.

Every page response carries these headers:

- `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'`
- `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, so the capability URL does not leak through the PR link
- `Cache-Control: no-store`
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`

Other rules for the pages:

- Every field is HTML-escaped.
- The access log redacts tokens (`/r/…`, `/s/…`).
- An unknown token answers the same 404 page as a revoked link, and counts toward the IP lockout.

**Management API** (decide tier for create and revoke, request tier for list):

- `GET /api/a2a/intake`
- `POST /api/a2a/intake` with `{ client, label }` returns `{ id, url, token }` once; the token is never shown again
- `POST /api/a2a/intake/<id>/revoke`

**CLI:**

- `dispatch a2a intake add <client> [--label "..."]` prints the URL
- `dispatch a2a intake list`
- `dispatch a2a intake revoke <id>`

Owner setup:

```
dispatch a2a clients add web-form --approve
dispatch a2a intake add web-form --label "Feature requests"
dispatch a2a listen --host 0.0.0.0 --tls-cert … --tls-key …   # or behind a tunnel/proxy with a public URL
```

**Storage:** two tables appended to `a2a.db` (`IF NOT EXISTS`, version unchanged):

- `intake_links(id, client, label, token_hash UNIQUE, created_by, created_at, revoked_at)`
- `intake_requests(id, link_id, task_id, status_hash UNIQUE, name, contact, notified_step, created_at)`

`task_id` is the A2A task id (the handoff's root message).

## Out of scope for phase 1

- Hosting through the relay (`/t/<thumbprint>`): the relay forwards port calls, not pages. This is phase 2 on app.dispatch.foo.
- Requester accounts, email verification, and a "my requests" list.
- Attachments, and custom form fields per link.
- Fixing the Needs you grouping bugs t-c854e7 and t-c873e4. Intake requests arrive as handoff proposals, so those fixes apply to them as is.

## Acceptance (phase 1)

- An owner can mint an intake link for an approved A2A client, list it, and revoke it.
- A person submitting the form gets a status URL. The team sees a draft with the `a2a` label and the person's name and contact in its fence, and a task-proposal gate in Needs you.
- The status page tracks Received → Accepted → In progress → In review → Done as the task moves, and shows Declined when the gate is declined.
- When the team asks the requester a question, the page shows it with a reply box, and a reply answers it.
- A revoked link and an unknown token both 404. A revoked link's existing status pages still read.
- Tokens never appear in the access log. Page headers include the CSP and `no-referrer`.
- `request.changed` posts once per step change and survives a restart without re-sending.

## As built (phase 1, commits e272129c..131a2cca)

- The store lives in `packages/a2a/src/store/sqlite.ts`.
- Pages, the step projection and the notifier live in `packages/server/src/a2a/intake.ts` and `intakePage.ts`.
- The listener routing is in `listener.ts`. It shares one `IpLimiter` with the A2A routes, so a lockout covers both.
- The API is in `routes.ts`, with tiers in `api.ts`. The CLI is `dispatch a2a intake`.
- Form posts must be `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`; multipart and other types are refused.
- The shared agent token is refused by the decide tier on every `/api/a2a/intake` route.
- There is no desktop UI for intake links yet. A follow-up could add one to the A2A settings, plus the `packages/client` function.

revision.title: Spec: end-to-end encrypted team content
revision.body:
# End-to-end encrypted team content

**Goal (Wyat, 2026-10-26):** "I just want it all to be encrypted e2e." Today only mail, state and a2a ops are sealed. Task, presence, agent, channel, memory and doc ops reach the relay (and a git remote) in the clear.

## Decision

Encrypt every content op body under a **team content key** (TCK) that only admitted members hold. The relay keeps seeing what it needs to authenticate machines, route and prune: the roster, key ops, and op headers (publisher, seq, hlc, type, size). It can no longer read any content.

**No relay change and no new op type.** The relay pins `@dispatch-foo/protocol` 0.3.0, whose verifier rejects unknown sealed types. Content ops keep their types and only their bodies change shape. The verifier hashes bodies opaquely (`contentProblem` checks only `sealed`/`to`).

## Envelope

A content op's body becomes:

```
{ "e2e": 1, "epoch": "<epoch id>", "nonce": b64, "ct": b64, ...clear hints }
```

- AES-256-GCM under the epoch's TCK. The AAD binds `dispatch-content-v1`, replica, seq and type, the same pattern as `seal.ts`.
- **Clear hints** are only what the relay or the pre-stage pass needs:
  - presence `kind`
  - presence `run` as `HMAC(TCK, runId)`, so the relay's per-run retention still groups by run
  - replica-presence `caps`, so capability gates work before a key is held
- Encryption happens at the one publish choke point (`FedStore.append`). Decryption happens before `evidenceOf` and `stageOne`. An op whose epoch key is missing is **parked** and restaged when the key arrives.
- `MAX_OP_BYTES - OP_ENVELOPE_BYTES` grows by the ciphertext overhead, so a task op still splits correctly.

## Epochs and keys

- An **epoch id** is the opHash of the roster op that opened it: the `content-e2e` switch, or a later `revoke`. Order comes from the roster fold, so every machine agrees and concurrent removals can never fork a counter.
- **The author of that roster op generates the epoch's 32-byte key** and grants it.
- **Grants** are sealed `state` ops (HPKE to each recipient's pinned `sealPub`, ≤256 per op) with payload `{grant: [{epoch, key}]}`.
  - Grants go only to members whose caps include `content-e2e`.
  - Each machine keeps its keyring at `<syncDir>/keys/content.json`, mode 0600.
- **Admit:** the admitting machine, and as a fallback any key holder, grants every epoch to the newcomer, so they can read the full history.
- **Revoke:** the revoker opens a new epoch and grants it to the remaining members. The removed machine keeps what it already had and gets nothing new.
- **Missing keys:** replica presence carries a clear `wants: [epoch]`. Any holder answers with a grant. This covers grants pruned after 30 days offline.

## Turning it on

- A new signed roster action `content-e2e`, committed like `transport`.
- **Allowed only when** every member and pending invitee has the `content-e2e` cap, and the legacy v1 window is closed. Legacy v1 copies would leak plaintext.
- Builds that don't know the action pause on it, instead of choking on ciphertext.
- After the switch, every new content op is encrypted. Builds with the cap add it to `BUILD_CAPS`.

## Surfaces

- **Settings → Team:** an "Encrypt everything end to end" control with readiness (who still needs an update). It shows the new relay disclosure once on.
- **CLI:** `dispatch team encrypt` (status, and on).
- **Disclosure text:** replace `RELAY_DISCLOSURE` (`teamKeys.ts`), `TeamSetupGroup.tsx` and the sealed-relay contract spec with what the relay sees now: roster, public keys, license, op headers and sizes, presence kind with an opaque run tag.
- **READMEs:** federation, server team and root.

## Known limits (say so in the UI and README)

- **History before the switch stays readable on the relay.** Board ops are never pruned. Purging it means re-founding the team, which is a follow-up.
- A removed member keeps what they received before removal.
- No forward secrecy inside an epoch. A stolen machine key exposes its epochs.
- **Metadata stays visible:** who is on the team, who published, when, op type, size. The license key stays in the roster, because the relay counts seats with it.
